lessons.title: Features and benefits
lessons.tip: A feature says what a product has: “a 20-hour battery.” A benefit says what it does for the customer: “you can use it all week without charging.” People buy benefits. First learn who your customer is and what they want, then turn each feature into a benefit.
sources: Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923, public domain): plain, specific, honest selling (concepts only)
US Federal Trade Commission truth-in-advertising principles (US government, public domain; summarized) and the AIDA model (concept)

lessons.title: One big idea
lessons.tip: Give your message one big idea. A value proposition says what you offer, who it is for and why it is better, in one clear sentence: “Quick, healthy lunches for busy students.” Too many ideas confuse people. If everything is important, nothing is.

lessons.title: Headlines that work
lessons.tip: A headline has one job: make people want to read the next line. Good headlines promise a benefit, raise a question, use a number or say something new. Keep them short and specific. Avoid vague words like “great” and “best” with no proof.
sources: Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923, public domain): plain, specific, honest selling (concepts only)
US Federal Trade Commission truth-in-advertising principles (US government, public domain; summarized) and the AIDA model (concept)

lessons.title: Honest claims
lessons.tip: Advertising must be true. Do not claim what you cannot prove, hide important costs or invent reviews. Say “up to” when results vary, and keep your proof ready. Honest copy builds trust, and trust sells again and again. Laws in many countries protect customers from false claims.
sources: Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923, public domain): plain, specific, honest selling (concepts only)
US Federal Trade Commission truth-in-advertising principles (US government, public domain; summarized) and the AIDA model (concept)

lessons.title: A short ad with AIDA
lessons.tip: AIDA is a simple plan for a short ad: Attention (a strong headline), Interest (a fact or story that fits the reader), Desire (show the benefit and how life improves) and Action (say what to do next). Keep each part short, and let each lead to the next.
sources: Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923, public domain): plain, specific, honest selling (concepts only)
US Federal Trade Commission truth-in-advertising principles (US government, public domain; summarized) and the AIDA model (concept)

lessons.title: Call to action
lessons.tip: A call to action (CTA) tells the reader exactly what to do next. Start with a strong verb: Buy, Join, Try, Book, Download. Be clear and specific: “Book your free class” beats “Click here.” Add a reason or a deadline if you can: “Book today and get a free lesson.”

lessons.title: Voice and tone
lessons.tip: Tone is how your words sound: friendly, serious, playful, expert. Choose a tone that fits the audience and the product, and keep it the same everywhere. Write as if you are talking to one person: use “you” and short words. Never sound rude, and never talk down to people.

lessons.title: Edit for clarity
lessons.tip: Edit your copy. Cut extra words. Replace vague words with concrete ones: “fast” becomes “ready in five minutes.” Use active verbs and short sentences. Read it aloud: if you stumble, rewrite. Check facts, names and prices last. One idea, one reader, one action.

lessons.title: Learn from your reader
lessons.tip: Good copy starts with the reader’s words, not yours. Read customer reviews and notes. Look for the problem they describe and the phrases they repeat. “The light is soft, so my eyes don’t hurt” tells you the benefit that matters. Use their words in your headline: it will sound true. Also note complaints; they show what you must answer.

lessons.title: Proof makes claims believable
lessons.tip: A claim like “soft, kind light” is easier to believe with proof. Use numbers (“4.6 stars from 1,200 buyers”), a guarantee (“30 days, free returns”), a short customer quote, or a clear demonstration. Be specific: “1,200 buyers” beats “thousands.” Never invent proof. If you have little proof, say less and be honest about what you can show.

lessons.title: Answer the reader’s doubts
lessons.tip: Before people buy, they have doubts: Is it worth the price? Will it work for me? What if I don’t like it? Good copy answers the doubts it can. lessons.title: Subject lines and short emails
lessons.tip: In email, the subject line decides whether the message is opened. Keep it short, specific and honest: “Free shipping until Friday” is better than “Amazing offer!!!” Use the reader’s name sparingly. In the body, put the main message first, use short paragraphs and give one clear button or link. Do not trick people with “Re:” or fake urgency.

Plain-language and honest-advertising guidance (ideas only; original wording; products in examples are invented)

lessons.title: Honest urgency and fine print

lessons.title: Persuasion principles, used honestly
lessons.tip: Research describes patterns in decisions: people follow what others do (social proof), dislike losses more than they like equal gains (loss aversion), and judge by comparison (anchoring). These can help you communicate, but they can also mislead. Use them honestly: show real numbers of real customers, describe a real cost of waiting, and compare with a fair alternative. If you would be uncomfortable explaining the technique to the customer, do not use it.

lessons.title: Taglines: rhythm and wordplay
lessons.tip: A tagline is a short line that a brand repeats. It should be easy to say and hard to forget. Rhythm helps: short words, a clear beat, perhaps repetition or a pair of contrasts. lessons.title: Write for other cultures
lessons.tip: Words and images do not travel unchanged. Translation moves the meaning; transcreation rebuilds the message so that it works in the new culture. A slogan that is lucky in one language may be rude or flat in another. Check colors, numbers, humor and symbols with someone from the culture. Keep the proposition constant and adapt the expression. Plan time for local review before launch.

lessons.title: Substantiation and disclosure
lessons.tip: Advertising claims must be truthful and supported by evidence you hold before you publish. A claim such as “clinically proven” needs a proper study and an accurate summary, not a small test described as proof. Disclose material limits clearly near the claim: sample size, “results vary,” conditions of an offer. Comparative claims must compare like with like. Paid endorsements must be disclosed as such. Rules differ by country, so follow your region’s rules and ask a qualified adviser. This is language practice, not legal advice.
